name: C++

facts.ai_role: The performance layer underneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp, and most inference runtimes are C++.
facts.steward: ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee

title: C++: The Performance Layer of Modern AI Systems
answer: C++ is a compiled, general purpose programming language first released in 1985 and standardized by ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21. In AI work it sits below the Python surface, where PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are written. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that it offers direct control over memory and speed, but that control comes with a steeper learning curve than Python and a smaller pool of AI specific tutorials.

sections.body: C++ is a compiled programming language first released in 1985, maintained by the ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee, with isocpp.org as its official site. Within AI it serves as the performance layer underneath the Python surface. PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are written in C++. The site's standardization pages show a committee that has completed technical work on C++26 and begun adding features to the C++29 working draft, so the language is actively evolving rather than frozen.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The facts identify C++ as the implementation language for training frameworks, inference runtimes and GPU kernels, which places it in model training, inference, serving and edge deployment. The site's CppCon 2026 keynote description points to efficiency under real space and time constraints as the language's central strength, and cites industry data from SlashData and IDC on sustained demand for programmers who can work at that level. Where an AI job needs predictable latency, tight memory control or direct hardware access, C++ is the natural choice. The site does not present it as a first language for data exploration or notebook style experimentation.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The official material does not set out a beginner curriculum, so the learning path has to be inferred from what the site does publish. The standardization pages assume familiarity with compiler flags, undefined behavior, memory safety profiles and library features such as std::simd and std::execution, which suggests that systems knowledge and some mathematics are useful prerequisites. GCC 16.1 release notes on the site mention C++20 enabled by default and modules still experimental behind -fmodules, so a newcomer also has to navigate toolchain choices. The annual developer survey is described as a ten minute one pager, which is the closest thing to an entry point the site offers.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The site documents an active ecosystem rather than a static one. Standards papers are mailed monthly, with entries for 2023 through 2025 visible across the category pages. Study groups SG14, covering low latency, games, embedded and financial trading, and SG19, covering machine learning, publish regular virtual meeting minutes. Compiler vendors ship features quickly, as shown by GCC 16.1 adding C++26 reflection, contracts and safety hardening. CppCon runs annually, with the 2026 edition starting September 12 in Aurora, Colorado, and the site also promotes talks, trip reports and an online AMA with Herb Sutter.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: The site frames C++ around efficiency, safety and control rather than rapid prototyping. The CppCon 2026 keynote description speaks of languages that operate under real space and time constraints, and the standards work on std::simd, std::execution and memory safety profiles is aimed at production performance. The JSON serialization talk notes that a full implementation was built using an experimental Bloomberg LLVM fork with reflective metaprogramming, which implies that some of the fastest paths depend on tooling that is not yet standard. The cost of that performance is more ceremony, longer build and debug cycles, and features that are still arriving.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site supports the view that C++ is a current standard rather than a legacy choice. The keynote description cites SlashData and IDC data on sustained demand for professional programmers, especially those who know languages that can operate under real space and time constraints. The committee is still adopting features, with C++26 technical work complete as of March 2026 and the first C++29 additions voted in during June 2026. For someone choosing it for work, that points to ongoing relevance in performance critical AI infrastructure, though the site does not publish hiring numbers or salary data, so those questions remain open.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: The facts describe a layered arrangement in which C++ sits beneath Python. PyTorch's libtorch and TensorFlow's core are C++ components exposed to Python users, CUDA kernels are written in C++, and llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are C++ projects. The site's own material adds adjacent concerns rather than competing languages, including compiler work in GCC, an experimental Bloomberg LLVM fork, and standards features such as reflection and std::simd. The polyglot pattern is therefore one of Python for orchestration and research, C++ for the runtime and kernel layer, and GPU toolchains underneath both.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid about work in progress. Memory safety profiles are still being prototyped and targeted at C++29, and a proposal to systematically address all undefined behavior is only entering line by line telecon review. C++20 modules support in GCC 16.1 is still experimental and must be enabled with -fmodules. The blog post by Giovanni Dicanio shows that AI generated code review can produce confident but incorrect findings, which is a caution about tooling rather than the language. The official material does not offer a beginner tutorial, benchmark comparisons against other languages, or guidance on which AI frameworks a newcomer should start with.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
